what_happened: A SOC 2 effort involves two kinds of people who use the same words for different jobs. The security team designs, runs and fixes the controls and asks whether they would hold up against a real attack. The CPA firm, a licensed service auditor that must stay independent of the company, asks for evidence: it samples what happened, tests it against the stated criteria and reports exceptions. A Type I report speaks to the design of controls on one day; a Type II report speaks to design and operation over a period of time. Management describes the system and asserts that the controls meet the criteria; the auditor opines on that assertion. These points are general professional practice, restated here without quoting any standard, and need a practitioner's check before sign-off.
lesson: Secure and attested are different claims. Build and run the controls as the engineer, keep the evidence as if someone will test it, and let an independent auditor judge it. Do not expect one person to do both jobs, and do not read a clean report as proof of safety.

evidence.claim: The AICPA describes SOC engagements as a suite of services that CPAs may provide on a service organization's system-level controls, with the AICPA setting the professional standards
The AICPA's SOC 2 materials cover controls relevant to security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality or privacy
